summary: Defines three channel binding types for TLS, named tls-unique, tls-server-end-point and tls-unique-for-telnet, following RFC 5056. Based on implementation experience, it changes the original definition of tls-unique in the IANA registry. It is a Proposed Standard.

eli5.summary: Ties a login to the exact secure tunnel it happens in, so a thief cannot move it to a different tunnel.

questions: what is channel binding in tls
subtitle: Three ways to tie an application login to the exact TLS connection it runs over.

tldr.problem: RFC 5056 describes channel binding in general, and three TLS channel binding types had been registered with IANA. The 'tls-unique' registration did not match what the first implementer actually built, and the types had no single RFC to cite.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5929 re-registers 'tls-unique', 'tls-server-end-point' and 'tls-unique-for-telnet' with exact definitions based on TLS Finished messages or a hash of the server certificate. It also gives advice on which to use and requires TLS stacks to expose the data through an API.
tldr.outcome: It changes 'tls-unique' in a backwards-incompatible way, with warnings. It is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9266.

facts.label: tls-server-end-point hash
facts.value: SHA-256 if the certificate uses MD5 or SHA-1

facts.label: Hash undefined when
facts.value: Signature algorithm uses no hash or several

today: RFC 5929 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9266. It changed the IANA registrations of its three channel binding types, and tls-unique in particular differs from its original definition.

sections.title: Why Re-register the Types
sections.content:
After RFC 5056 ("On Channel Bindings") was published, three channel binding types for Transport Layer Security (TLS) were proposed, reviewed and added to the IANA registry: tls-unique, tls-server-end-point and tls-unique-for-telnet. It had become desirable to register them again through an RFC, to make them easier to reference and to correct them to match real implementations. The authors have transferred, or said they will transfer, ownership of the types to the IESG.

The RFC also gives advice on when to use which type, and describes an abstract API that TLS implementors should provide. It carries an explicit warning: the first implementor built and deployed something rather different from the original tls-unique registration, so the IETF adopted that form, which makes this a backwards-incompatible change.
sections.eli5: Three secret handshake ideas were written down, but one of them was written differently from how people actually did it. This document fixes the writing to match real life.

sections.title: The tls-unique Type
sections.content:
The channel binding data is the first TLS Finished message sent (the Finished struct, not the record layer message that contains it) in the most recent handshake of the TLS connection being bound. It is defined per connection, not per session, so it is specific to each connection even when session resumption is used. If renegotiation happens before the channel binding operation, the first Finished message of the latest, inner-most connection is used.

In a full handshake the first Finished message is sent by the client. In an abbreviated handshake (session resumption) it is sent by the server.

Because the data can change after a renegotiation, an authentication attempt can fail spuriously if the binding changes between the client starting authentication and the server processing its first message. To avoid this, server applications MUST NOT request TLS renegotiation during phases where application-layer authentication occurs, and client applications SHOULD NOT initiate renegotiation between the start and completion of authentication.

The server side is a requirement and the client side a recommendation because TLS APIs for requesting renegotiation typically exist on the server side, while many client TLS stacks do not give fine-grained control. Application protocols SHOULD be designed so that a server never needs to request renegotiation right before or during authentication.
sections.eli5: It is like a stamp made at the very start of your tunnel. If the tunnel gets rebuilt in the middle of signing in, the stamp changes and the sign-in fails by accident, so nobody should rebuild the tunnel then.

sections.title: The tls-server-end-point Type
sections.content:
The channel binding data is a hash of the TLS server's certificate, exactly as it appears octet for octet in the server's Certificate message, using the first element of the certificate_list. The reason for hashing is that some implementations track the binding in kernel-mode memory, which is often scarce.

The hash function is chosen from the certificate's signature algorithm:

  • If it uses a single hash function that is MD5 or SHA-1, use SHA-256.
  • If it uses a single hash function that is neither MD5 nor SHA-1, use that hash function.
  • If it uses no hash function or several, the channel bindings are undefined at this time.

Registration fields for this type include the binding type end-point and the owner IESG. The only material changes from the original registration are the owner, the contacts, the published specification and a note pointing to this document for applicability advice.
sections.eli5: Instead of stamping the tunnel itself, this one writes down a short fingerprint of the server's ID card. If the ID card is different, the fingerprint is different.

sections.title: The tls-unique-for-telnet Type
sections.content:
This type exists for a proposal to add a "StartTLS" extension to TELNET, with a channel binding extension for the TELNET AUTH mechanisms. In it, each side sends the other a message authentication code (MAC, called a "checksum" in the text) over its view of the channel bindings.

The client uses the TLS Finished messages sent by the client and the server, concatenated in that order in their clear text form, from the first TLS handshake to which the connection is bound. The server does the same in the opposite order, server first and then client. The type is only applicable to TELNET (RFC 854) and is available for all TLS connections.
sections.eli5: For the old Telnet program, both sides write down the two start-up stamps and compare their notes, each reading them in their own order.

sections.title: Choosing a Type and Required APIs
sections.content:
tls-unique is available for all TLS connections. tls-server-end-point is available only for cipher suites that use the Certificate handshake message, typically with PKIX. It is not available for suites such as TLS_PSK_WITH_* or TLS_DH_anon_WITH_*, nor for OpenPGP server certificates. On the other hand, tls-server-end-point works with existing server-side proxies ("concentrators") without changes, while tls-unique may need firmware or software updates to them.

Security frameworks such as GSS-API and SASL generally do not negotiate the binding type, so peers must agree in advance. The RFC RECOMMENDS that application protocols use tls-unique exclusively, except where server-side proxies are common. In that case a protocol MAY require tls-server-end-point when it is available and fall back to tls-unique. Application protocol specifications MUST name at least one mandatory-to-implement type, MAY define negotiation or out-of-band configuration, and SHOULD prefer tls-unique.

TLS implementations that support tls-unique or tls-unique-for-telnet MUST provide APIs for clients and servers to obtain the binding data for a connection. The RFC takes no position on the shape of the API. Implementations that support renegotiation SHOULD also let applications control when it can take place, for example through a callback.
sections.eli5: When more than one stamp type could work, both sides have to agree beforehand which one to use. The default pick is the stamp from the tunnel itself, unless a middleman box makes the ID-card fingerprint easier.

sections.title: The Backwards-Incompatible Change
sections.content:
The original tls-unique description was the client's Finished message from the first handshake of the connection, whether full or abbreviated, regardless of later renegotiations. The new definition matches the old one only when a single full handshake took place before application-layer authentication.

The RFC knows of at least one TLS implementation that exports tls-unique with the original semantics, but of no deployed application using it. Old and new implementations interoperate only when full handshakes are used and renegotiation is not used. The new definition also brings the spurious-failure risk described earlier, unless applications follow the renegotiation rules.
sections.eli5: The recipe was changed to match how the cooks really made it. Old and new versions only taste the same when the dish was made the simple way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 5056, RFC 5246 and RFC 5746 apply. TLS Finished messages are known to both endpoints and are cryptographically bound to the connection. With implementations that handle renegotiation correctly, each handshake is bound to the preceding one, so Finished messages can safely be used as a channel binding. Without secure renegotiation support, applications using tls-unique MUST ensure ChangeCipherSpec was used in every renegotiation before application-layer authentication and MUST discard anything learned from the server before authentication completes. The server certificate is also bound to the connection, so it suits an end-point binding.

On algorithm agility, tls-unique and tls-unique-for-telnet add no cryptography beyond TLS. tls-server-end-point adds a hash, but the choice is derived from the certificate's signature algorithm, so its agility comes from PKIX and TLS.

On disclosure, none of the types produces data that must be kept secret. The unique types can be expected to be private only when a confidentiality-protecting cipher suite is used. An active man-in-the-middle attacker already knows the Finished messages of both channels, which differ, so learns nothing new from disclosed binding data.
sections.eli5: The stamps are not secrets, and that is fine. What matters is that a person in the middle ends up with different stamps on each side, so the sign-in does not match.

cells: First Finished message of the most recent handshake
